questions.q: Identify the stanza(s) that serve as the exposition in "Ajamil and the Tigers" and list the three key elements of exposition established there.
questions.a: The first stanza (lines 1-10) is the exposition. It establishes: (1) characters — tiger people, tiger king, Ajamil, sheep dog; (2) setting — implied pasture/forest border; (3) conflict — tigers starving for 15 days because the new sheep dog prevents them from hunting. A wrong answer (e.g., citing the tiger king's attack as exposition) reveals the student confuses the inciting incident with the initial situation-setting.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the tiger king's return "with a black patch on his eye / His tail in a sling" marks the transition from rising action to climax, not the climax itself.
questions.a: The injured return shows the failure of the first confrontation (rising action peak) and sets up the king's new plan ("I've got it all planned"), which leads to the actual climax — the mass attack and capture by the sheep dog. A student who calls this the climax misses that the decisive confrontation (51 tigers captured at once) happens afterward, and the true turning point is the political negotiation that follows.

questions.q: Apply the concept of "dramatic irony" to the scene where the tiger king claims "We were coming to see you as friends." What does the reader know that Ajamil pretends not to know?
questions.a: The reader knows (from the first stanza) that the tigers explicitly came to eat the sheep ("won't let us get within a mile of meat"). The tiger king's lie is transparent. Ajamil's pretense of believing it is a calculated political act. A wrong answer (e.g., "Ajamil is fooled") shows the student misses the irony and the poem's central satire on performative diplomacy.

questions.q: Analyze how the narrative structure subverts the traditional fable structure. Compare the expected resolution of a fable with the actual resolution in the poem.
questions.a: Traditional fable: predator is defeated or reformed; moral order restored; clear lesson (e.g., "honesty wins"). This poem: predator is invited to dinner, signs a treaty, and shares the pond. The "moral" is cynical realism — "even tigers have got to eat some time." The structure follows fable beats (talking animals, conflict, resolution) but inverts the moral outcome. A student who says "the tigers become friends" misses the satirical subversion.

questions.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of the poem's resolution: "He is free to play a flute all day as well fed tigers and fat sheep drink from the same pond." Does this ending resolve the central conflict or merely manage it? Justify.
questions.a: It manages, not resolves. The conflict (tigers eating sheep) is suspended by a pact that requires continuous feeding of tigers ("gifts of sheep, leather jackets and balls of wool"). The shepherd's freedom ("play a flute") depends on sustaining the predators. This mirrors political appeasement. A student who calls it a "happy ending" fails to evaluate the unsustainable, cynical nature of the peace.

questions.q: Create a one-stanza alternative ending (4-6 lines) that follows a traditional fable structure — where the sheep dog's victory leads to a clear moral — and explain how it changes the poem's genre.
questions.a: Example: "The dog drove the tigers back to their den, / And guarded the flock again and again. / No treaties signed, no feasts at night, / Just honest watch till morning light. / The shepherd slept, his trust well placed, / For duty kept the herd safe." This shifts genre from political satire to moral fable. A poor answer keeps the treaty but adds a moral tag, showing inability to distinguish structural vs. thematic change.
